content: Fifth disease, also known as erythema infectiosum, is a mild rash illness caused by a viral infection, most commonly affecting school-aged children. The illness is characterized by a distinctive slapped cheek rash on the face and a lacy red rash on the trunk and limbs, which may occasionally itch. Before the rash appears, affected children may experience mild symptoms such as a low-grade fever, malaise, or cold-like symptoms. The illness is generally mild, and the rash typically resolves within 7 to 10 days. Historically, fifth disease has been referred to by various names, including erythema infectiosum (meaning infectious redness), human parvovirus B19 infection, slapped cheek syndrome, slap cheek, slap face, or slapped face. It is classified as the fifth of the classical childhood exanthems (skin rashes). In 1975, the causative agent of fifth disease was identified as parvovirus B19. Individuals infected with parvovirus B19 are contagious during the early stages of the illness, before the rash appears. By the time the characteristic slapped cheek rash develops, the individual is usually no longer contagious and can return to school or childcare. This pattern of contagiousness differs from other rash illnesses, such as measles, where the individual remains contagious while the rash is present. The virus spreads through direct contact with respiratory secretions (e.g., saliva, sputum, or nasal mucus) of infected individuals, often before the rash appears when symptoms resemble a common cold. It can also be transmitted through blood products or vertically from mother to fetus. After exposure, symptoms typically develop within 4 to 14 days, though they may take up to 20 days to appear. Fifth disease is caused by human parvovirus B19, a linear, non-segmented, single-stranded DNA virus. The virus lacks a lipid envelope, making it resistant to physical inactivation by heat or detergents. Parvovirus infections are most common in children aged 5 to 15 years, with outbreaks frequently occurring in nurseries and schools. The infection is more prevalent during the late winter and spring months. Anyone can contract fifth disease, but once infected, individuals develop immunity to the virus. Most people acquire immunity during childhood. The disease is generally not serious unless the infected individual has underlying conditions, such as immune system problems, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, or anemia. Fifth disease is typically a mild illness that resolves on its own in otherwise healthy children and adults. However, complications can occur, including arthropathy (joint pain or swelling, particularly in the knees in children) and aplastic crisis due to the virus targeting rapidly growing erythroid progenitor cells. In rare cases, serious complications such as hydrops fetalis may develop if the infection occurs during pregnancy. The initial symptoms of fifth disease are usually mild and nonspecific, including fever, runny nose, headache, and nausea. These are followed by the development of the characteristic slapped cheek rash on the face, often accompanied by circumoral pallor (paleness around the mouth). Later, a lacy red rash may appear on the trunk and limbs. On physical examination, bright red cheeks are a hallmark symptom of the infection in children, giving rise to the name slapped cheek disease. The rash may occasionally extend over the bridge of the nose or around the mouth. In addition to red cheeks, children often develop a red, lacy rash on other parts of the body, with the upper arms and legs being the most common locations. A physician can often diagnose fifth disease based on the characteristic rash observed during a physical examination. In cases where confirmation is necessary, a blood test may be performed to detect antibodies to parvovirus B19. The presence of immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies indicates a recent infection. Testing for viral DNA is typically reserved for immunocompromised patients or those experiencing an aplastic crisis. Treatment for fifth disease is primarily symptomatic. Adults with joint pain and swelling may benefit from rest, activity restriction, and medications such as aspirin or ibuprofen to alleviate symptoms. Patients with complications may require additional interventions, such as blood transfusions or intravenous immune globulin therapy. There is no vaccine or specific medication to prevent parvovirus B19 infection. Frequent handwashing is recommended as a practical and likely effective measure to reduce the risk of infection.
